stem: A live production server is confirmed compromised and management intends to pursue criminal charges. A forensic examiner arrives while the system is still running. Which evidence should the examiner collect FIRST?

options.text: The contents of volatile memory (RAM) and current network connections
options.rationale: The order of volatility dictates capturing the most perishable data first; RAM and live network state disappear on shutdown, so they must be collected before disk or archived logs.

options.text: A bit-for-bit forensic image of the primary hard disk
options.rationale: Disk data is far less volatile than memory and survives a reboot; capturing it before RAM would sacrifice transient evidence that is gone once power is lost.

options.text: Archived syslog data stored on a remote log server
options.rationale: Archived logs are the least volatile evidence and can be collected last; prioritizing them wastes the window to capture memory.

options.text: Printed configuration documentation from the change management system
options.rationale: Static documentation is not volatile at all and is not time-sensitive; it is not a first-priority collection item.

stem: An administrator suspects malware on a workstation that may become evidence in a legal case. What should be done FIRST before any analysis?

options.text: Run an antivirus scan to identify and remove the malware
options.rationale: Running AV alters the system, may delete the very artifacts needed as evidence, and changes timestamps, destroying evidentiary value.

options.text: Reboot the machine to clear any active malicious processes
options.rationale: A reboot wipes volatile memory containing live evidence and can trigger anti-forensic cleanup, which is exactly the wrong first move.

options.text: Preserve the system by capturing volatile data and imaging the disk, documenting chain of custody
options.rationale: Preservation before analysis is the core forensic principle; capturing and documenting first protects both the evidence and its admissibility.

options.text: Open suspicious files to determine what the malware does
options.rationale: Opening files changes access timestamps and can execute payloads, contaminating the original evidence before it is preserved.

stem: During a trial, opposing counsel argues that a seized hard drive could have been tampered with between seizure and analysis. Which practice BEST refutes this claim?

options.text: A documented chain of custody recording every person who handled the drive and when
options.rationale: An unbroken chain of custody proves the evidence was continuously controlled and not altered or substituted, directly countering a tampering claim.

options.text: A signed statement from the analyst asserting the drive is genuine
options.rationale: A single unsupported assertion does not demonstrate continuous control and is weaker than documented custody plus hashing.

options.text: The fact that the drive was stored in a locked office
options.rationale: A locked location without documentation of who accessed it does not establish an unbroken, provable custody record.

options.text: A backup copy of the drive made after analysis
options.rationale: A post-analysis backup does not prove the evidence was untampered during the gap in question; it is not chain-of-custody evidence.

stem: Which standard of proof applies to a criminal investigation?

options.text: Preponderance of the evidence
options.rationale: Preponderance of the evidence ('more likely than not') is the civil standard, not the higher bar required for criminal cases.

options.text: Beyond a reasonable doubt
options.rationale: Criminal cases, which can result in loss of liberty, require the highest standard: beyond a reasonable doubt.

options.text: Clear organizational discretion
options.rationale: Organizational discretion characterizes administrative/internal investigations, not criminal ones.

options.text: Probable cause
options.rationale: Probable cause is the threshold to obtain a warrant or make an arrest, not the standard for a criminal conviction.

stem: A forensic examiner has seized a laptop and needs to analyze its contents. What is the BEST way to conduct the analysis while preserving admissibility?

options.text: Analyze a hashed, bit-for-bit forensic image while the original is stored securely
options.rationale: Working from a verified image keeps the original pristine and lets the examiner prove, via matching hashes, that the analyzed copy is identical to the original.

options.text: Analyze the original drive directly to avoid copy errors
options.rationale: Working on the original risks altering it and destroys the ability to demonstrate the evidence is unchanged, undermining admissibility.

options.text: Make a simple file-copy of the user's documents and examine those
options.rationale: A logical file copy misses slack space, deleted files, and metadata, and is not a forensically sound, verifiable image.

options.text: Boot the laptop normally and browse the file system
options.rationale: Booting the original modifies numerous files and timestamps, contaminating the evidence.

stem: An analyst plans to introduce server log files at trial to show an intrusion occurred. Which category of evidence do the log files BEST represent?

options.text: Documentary evidence
options.rationale: Logs are written/recorded information offered to prove a fact, which is the definition of documentary evidence.

options.text: Real (physical) evidence
options.rationale: Real evidence is a tangible object like the physical drive; the log content itself is documentary, not physical.

options.text: Testimonial evidence
options.rationale: Testimonial evidence is a witness's sworn statement; the logs are records, though an analyst may testify about them.

options.text: Demonstrative evidence
options.rationale: Demonstrative evidence is an illustrative aid such as a diagram; raw logs are the underlying records, not an aid explaining them.

stem: Defense counsel objects that automatically generated firewall logs are inadmissible hearsay. Which argument BEST supports admitting them?

options.text: They qualify under the business-records exception because they are routinely generated in the normal course of operations
options.rationale: Computer-generated records created routinely in the ordinary course of business commonly qualify under the business-records exception to the hearsay rule.

options.text: Logs are never considered hearsay under any circumstances
options.rationale: This overstates the rule; logs can raise hearsay concerns and rely on an exception, so a blanket claim is incorrect.

options.text: The analyst personally witnessed each logged event
options.rationale: Logs are generated automatically, not personally witnessed; this misstates how the evidence was produced.

options.text: Hearsay rules do not apply to digital evidence
options.rationale: Hearsay rules can apply to digital evidence; admissibility depends on exceptions like business records, not on a special exemption.

stem: An organization is looking into whether an employee violated an internal acceptable-use policy, with potential discipline but no lawsuit or law enforcement involvement. This is MOST accurately classified as which type of investigation?

options.text: Administrative investigation
options.rationale: An internal policy/HR matter with the lowest standard and organizational discretion is an administrative investigation.

options.text: Criminal investigation
options.rationale: No violation of law or law enforcement is involved, so the criminal category and its high standard do not apply.

options.text: Civil investigation
options.rationale: A civil matter involves a dispute between parties seeking damages/relief, not an internal disciplinary review.

options.text: Regulatory investigation
options.rationale: A regulatory investigation involves an external industry regulator, which is not present in a purely internal policy review.

stem: Which forensic principle holds that any contact between two entities leaves a trace that may be recovered?

options.text: Locard's exchange principle
options.rationale: Locard's exchange principle states that every contact leaves a trace, underpinning the expectation that intruder artifacts can be recovered.

options.text: The best evidence rule
options.rationale: The best evidence rule concerns preferring originals over copies, not the transfer of trace artifacts.

options.text: The Daubert standard
options.rationale: The Daubert standard governs the admissibility of expert/scientific testimony, not the concept of trace exchange.

options.text: The chain of custody
options.rationale: Chain of custody is the documented handling record of evidence, not a principle about trace transfer.

stem: Which factor is LEAST relevant to whether a piece of digital evidence will be deemed admissible?

options.text: The dollar value of the storage device the evidence resides on
options.rationale: The monetary value of the media has no bearing on admissibility, which turns on relevance, reliability, and lawful collection.

options.text: Whether the evidence was collected lawfully
options.rationale: Lawful (permissible) collection is a core admissibility requirement; unlawfully obtained evidence may be excluded.

options.text: Whether the evidence is relevant to the matter at hand
options.rationale: Relevance is a fundamental admissibility criterion; irrelevant evidence is excluded.

options.text: Whether the evidence is reliable and authentic
options.rationale: Reliability/authenticity is essential to admissibility; evidence that cannot be authenticated may be rejected.

stem: A help-desk technician discovers evidence of fraud on an employee's computer that may lead to prosecution. The technician wants to help the investigation. What should the technician be instructed to do FIRST?

options.text: Stop touching the system and secure it so trained personnel can preserve evidence
options.rationale: Untrained interaction can destroy evidence and break chain of custody; securing the scene and escalating preserves both the evidence and its admissibility.

options.text: Copy the incriminating files to a USB drive for safekeeping
options.rationale: An ad-hoc copy by untrained staff alters timestamps, lacks forensic soundness, and breaks chain of custody.

options.text: Email the files to the security team as attachments
options.rationale: Emailing files is not forensically sound, changes metadata, and does not preserve the original evidence properly.

options.text: Delete the files to prevent the employee from destroying them
options.rationale: Deleting evidence is destruction of evidence and is never appropriate; it also removes what the case depends on.

stem: Which standard of proof is used in most civil cases?

options.text: Beyond a reasonable doubt
options.rationale: This is the higher criminal standard, not the civil standard.

options.text: Preponderance of the evidence
options.rationale: Civil cases are decided on a preponderance of the evidence — the claim is more likely true than not.

options.text: Absolute certainty
options.rationale: No legal proceeding requires absolute certainty; this is not a recognized standard.

options.text: Beyond a shadow of a doubt
options.rationale: This is a colloquial phrase, not a legal standard of proof.

stem: When proving the contents of a signed contract in court, which item does the best evidence rule prefer be presented?

options.text: The original signed contract document
options.rationale: The best evidence rule favors the original document over copies or descriptions when proving its contents.

options.text: A photocopy of the contract
options.rationale: A copy is disfavored when the original is available, per the best evidence rule.

options.text: A witness's recollection of what the contract said
options.rationale: A secondhand recollection is weaker than the original and may also raise hearsay concerns.

options.text: A summary memo describing the contract terms
options.rationale: A summary is not the original and does not satisfy the best evidence rule for proving contents.

stem: After imaging a suspect drive, an examiner wants to prove months later that the working image is identical to the original at the time of seizure. Which practice BEST provides this assurance?

options.text: Computing a cryptographic hash of the original at acquisition and re-hashing the image to confirm they match
options.rationale: Matching cryptographic hashes taken at acquisition and later demonstrate the image is a bit-for-bit, unaltered copy of the original.

options.text: Storing the original drive in an evidence locker only
options.rationale: Secure storage helps custody but does not itself prove the working image equals the original content.

options.text: Keeping detailed handwritten notes of the analysis steps
options.rationale: Notes document process but do not cryptographically verify that the image matches the original.

options.text: Password-protecting the image file
options.rationale: A password protects access but provides no proof the image content is unchanged or matches the original.

stem: A financial regulator opens an inquiry into whether a bank failed to retain transaction records as required by law. This is MOST accurately classified as which type of investigation?

options.text: Regulatory investigation
options.rationale: An inquiry driven by an external industry regulator enforcing legal/compliance requirements is a regulatory investigation.

options.text: Administrative investigation
options.rationale: Administrative investigations are internal policy/HR matters, not externally driven by a regulator.

options.text: Criminal investigation
options.rationale: Absent a criminal charge and law enforcement, this is a regulatory rather than criminal matter.

options.text: Civil investigation
options.rationale: A civil investigation involves a private dispute between parties, not a regulator enforcing compliance.

stem: Evidence was genuine and properly collected, but the log of who handled it has a two-day gap with no record of custody. What is the MOST likely consequence?

options.text: The evidence may be ruled inadmissible due to the broken chain of custody
options.rationale: A gap in custody undermines the ability to prove the evidence was not altered or substituted, which can render even genuine evidence inadmissible.

options.text: The evidence is automatically admissible because it is genuine
options.rationale: Genuineness alone does not overcome a custody gap; admissibility also requires demonstrable, unbroken handling.

options.text: The gap has no effect as long as the hash still matches
options.rationale: A matching hash helps integrity claims but does not fully cure an undocumented custody gap that opposing counsel can exploit.

options.text: The evidence must be recollected from the original scene
options.rationale: Recollection is usually impossible after the fact and is not the standard consequence; the immediate risk is inadmissibility.

stem: In the digital forensics process (identification, preservation, collection, examination, analysis, presentation), which phase comes FIRST after identifying relevant evidence?

options.text: Preservation
options.rationale: Once evidence is identified, preservation comes next to protect it from alteration before it is collected and examined.

options.text: Analysis
options.rationale: Analysis occurs later, after evidence has been preserved, collected, and examined.

options.text: Presentation
options.rationale: Presentation is the final phase, delivering findings, not an early step.

options.text: Examination
options.rationale: Examination follows collection; it cannot precede preservation of the identified evidence.

stem: Following the order of volatility, which of the following data sources is the LEAST volatile and can be collected last?

options.text: Archived backup tapes stored offsite
options.rationale: Backups/archives are the most stable, long-lived data and sit at the least-volatile end of the collection order.

options.text: CPU registers and cache
options.rationale: CPU registers and cache are the most volatile data and must be collected first, not last.

options.text: Contents of RAM
options.rationale: RAM is highly volatile and is lost on power-off, so it is collected early, not last.

options.text: Active network connections
options.rationale: Live network state is transient and disappears quickly, so it ranks near the top of the volatility order.

stem: An examiner prepares an animated timeline reconstructing the sequence of an attacker's actions to help the jury understand complex log data. This aid BEST fits which evidence category?

options.text: Demonstrative evidence
options.rationale: An illustrative aid created to help explain other evidence to the trier of fact is demonstrative evidence.

options.text: Real evidence
options.rationale: Real evidence is a tangible object; a created timeline is an aid, not a physical item from the scene.

options.text: Documentary evidence
options.rationale: Documentary evidence is the underlying records (like the logs); the animation explaining them is demonstrative.

options.text: Testimonial evidence
options.rationale: Testimonial evidence is a witness's sworn statement, not a visual aid.

stem: A running server contains an in-memory malware payload that never writes itself to disk. Rebooting is being considered to restore service. From an evidence standpoint, what is the MOST important consideration?

options.text: Capture a memory image before rebooting, because the payload exists only in RAM and will be lost on power cycle
options.rationale: Memory-resident-only malware is destroyed by a reboot; capturing volatile memory first is essential to preserve the sole copy of the evidence.

options.text: Reboot immediately since the malware will be captured in the next disk backup
options.rationale: A disk backup cannot capture memory-only malware that never touches disk; rebooting would destroy the evidence.

options.text: Run antivirus first to quarantine the payload as evidence
options.rationale: AV quarantine alters the system and may not preserve a forensically sound copy of the live memory state.

options.text: Nothing special is needed because disk evidence is equivalent to memory evidence
options.rationale: Disk and memory evidence are not equivalent; memory holds transient artifacts that disk does not, especially for fileless malware.
